\section*{AP \({ }^{\text {® }}\) CALCULUS AB \\ 2008 SCORING GUIDELINES (Form B)}

\section*{Question 6}

Consider the closed curve in the \(x y\)-plane given by
\[
x^{2}+2 x+y^{4}+4 y=5 .
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Show that \(\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-(x+1)}{2\left(y^{3}+1\right)}\).
\item[(b)] Write an equation for the line tangent to the curve at the point \((-2,1)\).
\item[(c)] Find the coordinates of the two points on the curve where the line tangent to the curve is vertical.
\item[(d)] Is it possible for this curve to have a horizontal tangent at points where it intersects the \(x\)-axis? Explain your reasoning.
\item[(a)] \(2 x+2+4 y^{3} \frac{d y}{d x}+4 \frac{d y}{d x}=0\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left(4 y^{3}+4\right) \frac{d y}{d x}=-2 x-2 \\
& \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-2(x+1)}{4\left(y^{3}+1\right)}=\frac{-(x+1)}{2\left(y^{3}+1\right)}
\end{aligned}
\]
\item[(b)] \(\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{(-2,1)}=\frac{-(-2+1)}{2(1+1)}=\frac{1}{4}\)
Tangent line: \(y=1+\frac{1}{4}(x+2)\)
\item[(c)] Vertical tangent lines occur at points on the curve where \(y^{3}+1=0\) (or \(y=-1\) ) and \(x \neq-1\).
On the curve, \(y=-1\) implies that \(x^{2}+2 x+1-4=5\), so \(x=-4\) or \(x=2\).
Vertical tangent lines occur at the points (-4, -1) and (2, -1).
\item[(d)] Horizontal tangents occur at points on the curve where \(x=-1\) and \(y \neq-1\).
The curve crosses the \(x\)-axis where \(y=0\).
\[
(-1)^{2}+2(-1)+0^{4}+4 \cdot 0 \neq 5
\]
No, the curve cannot have a horizontal tangent where it crosses the \(x\)-axis.
\end{itemize}

\(3:\left\{\begin{array}{c}1: y=-1 \\ 1: \text { substitutes } y=-1 \text { into the } \\ \text { equation of the curve } \\ 1: \text { answer }\end{array}\right.\)
